extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kant; interested in teleology, moral philosophy, and theodicy)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Kant's criteria and argumentative moves about physical teleology, moral teleology, and the moral proof of God from a section of the Critique of the Power of Judgment. Focus is on what counts as grounds, limits, and implications for assuming a final purpose and a moral World-Cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical Teleology is insufficient to establish Deity
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical Teleology (physico-theology) impels us to seek a Theology but cannot itself produce one; it is only serviceable as a preparation (propaedeutic) for Theology and inadequate alone for furnishing a concept of a Deity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that even with the fullest empirical investigation of purposive arrangements in nature, physical Teleology cannot reveal whether an Understanding (intelligent Cause) has a final design; thus physical Teleology at best prepares us for theological speculation but cannot supply the theological principle itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative explanations of apparent purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent teleology in nature can be (a) explained away as a deception of the Judgement leading to mechanistic explanations, (b) assimilated to Idealism/Pantheism/Spinozism (unity of substance), (c) ascribed to many intelligent beings, or (d) ascribed to a single intelligent Cause — but empirical principles alone cannot determine which.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage warns that empirical observation of purposive combinations cannot decide the unity of purpose or whether a single intelligent Cause exists; thus empirical grounds are indeterminate for theological conclusions about a supreme Understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final purpose required for a teleological system
rubrics_metrics.description: To form teleological principles and a concept of a Supreme Understanding as Cause, Reason must supply a final purpose; without such a final purpose one can have at most an 'artistic Understanding' for scattered purposes but no overarching Wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical Reason cannot derive the concept of a Deity or a final purpose solely from nature; pure practical Reason must provide the idea of a final purpose to make teleological judgement systemic and serviceable for Theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man (rational beings) as the final purpose of creation (moral Teleology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common human Reason judges that the existence of the world would be purposeless without rational beings (men); thus the final purpose of creation must be man (or rational beings) under moral laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues this is not because of cognitive contemplation or pleasure but because moral worth (good will) makes existence valuable; this is the a priori principle grounding moral Teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good will as the sole source of absolute worth
rubrics_metrics.description: The worth which a rational being alone can give to himself—consisting in what he does, how and according to what principles he acts, in freedom of desire—is a good will, and only a good will gives absolute worth that can ground a final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant contrasts moral worth with contingent goods (talent, happiness); only the good will qualifies a being as final purpose for the creation in a way that justifies teleological judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law prescribes a final purpose a priori (highest good)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law, as the formal rational condition of the use of our freedom, obliges us a priori to strive toward a final purpose — the highest good (summum bonum), which combines morality (worthiness) with happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The highest good is defined as the combination of the greatest welfare (happiness) of rational beings with the highest condition of the good in itself (morality); morality is a priori certain, while happiness is empirically conditioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of postulating a moral World-Cause (God) for practicability of the final purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the harmony of happiness with morality cannot be guaranteed by mere natural causes, practical Reason requires assuming a moral World-Cause (an Author of the world) to make the final purpose practicable — hence a moral proof of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical (not speculative/theoretical) argument: to make the moral law's demand to promote the highest good consistent with the possibility of its realization, we must posit a God who can harmonize nature with moral ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest Good (summum bonum) as criterion for practical judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The summum bonum is the objective final purpose that practical Reason enjoins: universal happiness conjoined with morality most accordant to law; it functions as the practical aim that requires the assumption of a moral Author of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant notes that while morality stands a priori, the empirical possibility of happiness aligning with morality cannot be shown theoretically; the summum bonum motivates postulating conditions (e.g., God, immortality) that render the aim practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: moral proof yields only practical (subjective) reality, not theoretical cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of a final purpose and of a moral Author of the world has practical reality for Reason (it is necessary for guiding action), but this does not amount to theoretical knowledge or cognition of God; we cannot cognize the supreme Being theoretically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant stresses that the concept of God gained from moral Teleology is transcendent for speculative Reason; it gives practical reality to moral aims but does not permit determinate theoretical claims about God's inner nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of the Supreme Cause inferred analogically from moral Teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Insofar as we infer properties necessary for an Author who can secure the final purpose, we ascribe analogically attributes such as all-knowing, all-mighty, all-good, just, Wisdom, Eternity, and Omnipresence to the Supreme Being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These attributes are posited because they are the conditions required to make the world conform to a moral final purpose; Kant cautions that such attributions are analogical and should not be taken as literal theoretical knowledge of God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral feelings motivate belief in a moral legislating Being
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate moral sentiments—gratitude, obedience, humiliation and the felt need to give account—lead a person disposed to moral feeling to conceive of a moral Intelligence or Supreme Lord to whom duty and gratitude can be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subjective moral disposition is presented as a psychological/practical ground for representing a morally-legislating Being; Kant treats this as a legitimate moral incentive, not a speculative proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between reflective and determinant judgement in teleology and theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflective judgement (practical/reflexive) can combine moral and physical teleology to justify thinking of a final purpose and a moral Author for practical ends, whereas determinant (theoretical) judgement cannot determine such a Being theoretically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant uses this distinction to explain how Theology can be established for the sake of practical Reason (reflective/prescriptive use) but resists apodictic theoretical demonstration; the appeal is to the needs of practical deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about analogy and anthropomorphism in ascribing divine properties
rubrics_metrics.description: We can think properties of the highest Being only according to analogy; applying predicates derived from experience risks anthropomorphism and does not yield true theoretical knowledge of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant insists the use of such concepts is to regulate human moral will and judgement, not to assert claims about the inner constitution of the divine; examples show we name causes after concepts of their effects without claiming identity of mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical necessity of God does not alter the binding force of the moral law if one denies God
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral proof does not mean the obligation of the moral law depends on belief in God; one who denies God is not thereby freed from moral obligation — denial only affects the practical aim of realizing the final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant explains that the moral law commands unconditionally; absence of belief in God would at most force one to give up aiming at the final purpose (the summum bonum), but not to abandon duty itself.
